{"id": "00000000-0000-4000-8000-67b7821073f5", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "What is the difference between an Application Load Balancer and a Network Load Balancer?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}

{"id": "00000000-0000-4000-8000-973fe0d9c6b7", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "thinking", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "This is a general AWS conceptual question rather than something specific to the DevOps Agent product, so I can just answer it directly from what I know without needing to look anything up.\n\n"}]}

{"id": "00000000-0000-4000-8000-fd46d31fd9e3", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Here's how the two compare. The main difference is the OSI layer each one works at.

| | **Application Load Balancer (ALB)** | **Network Load Balancer (NLB)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Layer** | Layer 7 (application) | Layer 4 (transport) |
| **Protocols** | HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC, WebSocket | TCP, UDP, TLS, TCP_UDP |
| **Routing** | Content-based: host, path, headers, query strings, HTTP methods, source IP | Based on IP, port and protocol only |
| **Performance** | Good for web traffic. Adds some latency because it inspects requests. | Very high throughput and ultra-low latency. Handles sudden, volatile traffic spikes well. |
| **Client IP** | Passed in the `X-Forwarded-For` header | Preserved as the source IP in most target configurations |
| **Static IPs** | No. It uses a DNS name, and its IPs can change. | Yes. It gives one static IP per AZ and supports Elastic IPs. |
| **Targets** | Instances, IPs, Lambda functions | Instances, IPs, and ALBs (to put static IPs in front of an ALB) |
| **TLS** | Terminates TLS and supports SNI | Terminates TLS or passes it through to targets |
| **Auth and security** | Built-in OIDC/Cognito authentication, AWS WAF integration, redirects and fixed responses | Security groups are supported. It has no WAF and no HTTP-level features. |
| **PrivateLink** | Not directly | Yes. NLB is the usual front end for a VPC endpoint service. |

**Choose an ALB when:**
- You're serving HTTP/HTTPS or gRPC, such as web apps, APIs or microservices.
- You need path-based or host-based routing, for example `/api` to one service and `/web` to another.
- You want WAF, user authentication, or Lambda targets.

**Choose an NLB when:**
- You need very high performance or low latency, or you expect millions of requests per second.
- You're handling non-HTTP protocols such as raw TCP or UDP, for example gaming, IoT, DNS or custom protocols.
- Clients or firewalls need static or allow-listable IP addresses.
- You're exposing a service through AWS PrivateLink.

**Using both:** You can put an NLB in front of an ALB. This gives you static IPs and PrivateLink support, plus Layer 7 routing.

If you'd like, I can look at the load balancers in your connected AWS accounts and check which type each one uses.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
